summary.title: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names
summary.one_liner: A list of common but wrong assumptions software makes about personal names, such as single canonical names, fixed lengths, ASCII-only characters, and first/last name fields, with a warning against naive name handling.
keywords: why names are hard to store
takeaways: Many common assumptions about names (one canonical name, fixed length, ASCII only, first and last name fields) are wrong.
Names can change, have prefixes or suffixes, contain numbers, and follow varied ordering and naming conventions across cultures.
Different systems and data entry operators will not reliably produce identical strings for the same person's name.
Avoid schemas like first_name and last_name, and accept any string a person gives as their name.
summary.summary: This classic essay by Patrick McKenzie responds to a complaint about a system rejecting a person's last name as containing invalid characters. He argues that software routinely mishandles names and then lists about five dozen assumptions developers make that are false, grouped roughly around uniqueness, length, character sets, case, ordering, change over time, and cultural differences. The list is written informally and uses personal anecdotes and examples from many countries rather than code or formal specifications. It works as a checklist for reviewing name handling in systems.
